The nesting comes from Action Controller's parameter wrapper. For JSON requests it copies the params under a key derived from the controller or model name, limited to the model's attribute names when a model is found.

`actionpack/lib/action_controller/metal/params_wrapper.rb`
`actionpack/lib/action_controller/railtie.rb`
`railties/lib/rails/application/configuration.rb`

`params_wrapper.rb` builds the wrapper key and filters the attributes (`_wrapper_key`, `_extract_parameters`, `_default_wrap_model`), and `railtie.rb` wires it in with `wrap_parameters format: [:json]` when `wrap_parameters_by_default` is on. `configuration.rb` is where that default is switched on by `load_defaults`; I found it by search but did not open it, so that attribution is less certain than the first two.

`actionpack/lib/action_controller/metal/params_wrapper.rb`
`actionpack/lib/action_controller/railtie.rb`

This is Rails' `ParamsWrapper` module. When a JSON request arrives and wrapping is enabled, it copies the top-level params under a key derived from the controller name (for example `user` for `UsersController`). If the model class responds to `attribute_names`, it limits the copy to those column names (`params_wrapper.rb:118-119`). It skips wrapping if the client already sent that key (`params_wrapper.rb:294`). `railtie.rb:84` enables it for JSON by default when `wrap_parameters_by_default` is set.

`railties/lib/rails/application/configuration.rb`

Rails' `ParamsWrapper` module copies the JSON body into a hash keyed by the controller's model name (`_wrapper_key`). When the model class responds to `attribute_names`, it limits that copy to those columns (`Options#include`, lines 108-139). The original top-level keys stay in place. The railtie turns the wrapping on for JSON requests by default through `wrap_parameters_by_default`. I matched `configuration.rb` by grep but did not open it, so its exact role is unverified.

The `ParamsWrapper` module in `params_wrapper.rb` copies JSON request params under a key named after the controller's model (the `_wrapper_key`), and when no model is set it limits them to `attribute_names`, which is why only column names appear under that key. The railtie and the `load_defaults` configuration turn this on by default for JSON, and `base.rb` mixes the module into `ActionController::Base`.

The primitive is `ActiveSupport::Concurrency::ShareLock`. Its `start_exclusive(compatible: [], no_wait: ...)` and `stop_exclusive(compatible: [])` methods let a thread that already holds a share yield that share to compatible activity, so an exclusive request can't deadlock against it. I identified this from the signatures in the index and didn't read the method bodies, so the deadlock-avoidance behaviour is inferred from those signatures, not confirmed in the code.

`ShareLock` in Active Support is the reader-writer primitive. Its `exclusive` and `yield_shares` methods let a thread give up its shared hold to compatible activity, so an upgrade attempt cannot deadlock.

`share_lock.rb` implements the lock: many threads call `start_sharing`, one waits in `start_exclusive` or `exclusive`, and `yield_shares` releases the caller's own share temporarily. `share_lock_test.rb` exercises these behaviours.

The primitive is `ActiveSupport::Concurrency::ShareLock`, a share/exclusive lock where `yield_shares` releases the caller's shared hold so that compatible work can proceed.

The markup is a comment, `<!-- '"` -->`, which closes any open quote or attribute before the form. It is prepended to `form_tag` and `button_to` output, but only when `config.action_view.prepend_content_exfiltration_prevention` is enabled, which defaults to `false`.

The helper defines `CLOSE_QUOTES_COMMENT` and `prevent_content_exfiltration`, which prepends that comment to the generated form HTML, so any unclosed quote or attribute an attacker injected ends inside the comment instead of capturing the form's contents. `form_tag_helper.rb` and `url_helper.rb` call it when building forms, `railtie.rb` wires up the config flag, and `configuring.md` documents the option.

The prepend is off by default; the railtie sets `prepend_content_exfiltration_prevention` to `false`, so it must be enabled through configuration.

The mechanism is Active Job's continuations. A worker shutdown sets the adapter's `stopping?` flag, the job's next checkpoint raises `Continuation::Interrupt`, and `resume_job` calls `retry_job` with `resume_options` (default `wait: 5.seconds`). The serialized continuation, including the current step and its cursor, is stored in the job data and restored on deserialize.

`activejob/lib/active_job/continuable.rb`
`activejob/lib/active_job/continuation.rb`
`activejob/lib/active_job/continuation/step.rb`
`activejob/lib/active_job/exceptions.rb`

`continuable.rb` holds the shutdown check (`checkpoint!`), the rescue that turns an interrupt into `resume_job`, and the `retry_job` call with the delay. `continuation.rb` defines the `Interrupt` exception, the resume options, and the serialized progress. `step.rb` stores the cursor that gets carried into the next run. `exceptions.rb` implements `retry_job`, which does the actual re-enqueue.

The job is re-enqueued by ActiveJob's continuation mechanism, which is in the `activejob/` component.

1. `activejob/lib/active_job/continuable.rb`: `checkpoint!` raises an interrupt when `queue_adapter.stopping?` is true. `resume_job` then calls `retry_job(**resume_options)`, which re-enqueues the job after a delay and carries the serialized `continuation` and `resumptions` through `serialize`/`deserialize`.
2. `activejob/lib/active_job/continuation.rb`: defines `Continuation::Interrupt`, the `resume_options` default of `{ wait: 5.seconds }`, and the `Continuation.new(job, serialized_progress)` that restores completed steps and the current step's cursor.
3. `activejob/lib/active_job/continuation/step.rb`: holds each step's cursor. `checkpoint!` and `set!(cursor)` store progress, so the next run resumes from that cursor.
4. `activejob/lib/active_job/queue_adapters/async_adapter.rb`: provides the `stopping?` signal that the shutdown path sets, though I did not open this file to confirm the details.
5. `activejob/lib/active_job/exceptions.rb`: provides `retry_job`, which performs the delayed re-enqueue, though I did not open this file either.

The reason is that `checkpoint!` turns a shutdown signal into a `Continuation::Interrupt`, which `continue` rescues and passes to `resume_job`; that calls `retry_job` with a delay, and the serialized progress in the job data lets the next execution pick up from the saved cursor.
